I had a paper on the arXiv today on the formalization of the stability of the two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) potential, and on the identification of a non-trivial error in the physics literature through the process of formalization. The 2HDM is an extension of the Standard Model of particle physics and something studied by particle phenomenologists.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08139

Do you have other notable papers whose result can be formalized with the current state of Mathlib and PhysLib? How long did it take to formalize the stability of the 2HDM? Also, can't find a GitHub link of the formalization.
If you click the names of the results in the code blocks it will take you to the corresponding result in PhysLib.

Concerning other notable papers - there are certainly very many similar papers to this one. This comes from particle phenomenology in which the mathematical machinery does not tend to be as sophisticated as in high-energy theory or mathematical physics. Thus they are more within reach of what is currently in Mathlib and PhysLib.

Anything that looks specifically at extending the scalar sector of the Standard Model should be doable right now. I suspect these sorts of papers come out weekly if not daily (although not as widely cited as the one I looked at). Indeed here is one from today: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.07608

A very nice read! I appreciate the dual-column approach.
What is your feeling about the overall "correctness" of the literature? From what I know about formalization projects in mathematics, most errors in papers are easily patched or made correct with some additional minor assumption.

For this specific paper: the error is more fundamental in that it is actually one of the main theorems is provably false, not just that the proof is incorrect. This I do not think has an easy patch.

I think in the physics literature there are likely very many papers with errors, the majority of which will be easy to patch, but some of which will not be. I think the only way to really test this is to do a random sample, but that would require a lot of work.

I think the real problem is that in many areas of physics (including particle phenomenology where this paper is from) the review process does not include a verification of the underlying mathematics. In other words physics papers appearing in certain journals have only ever had their authors check the underlying mathematics.

nice result :tada:
In phenomenology, how important is it to have a sufficient condition like this for stability? I'm guessing that necessary condition is good in that it reduces the parameter space, but what about a sufficient condition?

I think it is important in the following sense:

If I have specific potential I am interested in and I want to check if it is stable or not, I can use these sufficient conditions to reduce the complexity of the condition that I need to check. This is especially useful in the complicated potentials like this one which involve many terms.

However, it should be noted that the incorrect result is about the stability of the full 2HDM potential (including the quadratic terms), what people sometimes do is assume that the potential is stable only due to the quartic term - this doesn't break any results there.
by "specific potential" do you mean some values suggested by experiments? so it's a kind of sanity check for the model?
That - or one where you haven't chosen all of the parameters, but have chosen some constraints on them, for example if you are interested in potentials with a certain symmetry breaking pattern etc.
I see, there are such constrained cases. thanks!

Let me attempt to give the (Lean) executive summary of the error in https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0605184.

Let J₂ J₄ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) → ℝ be functions such that J₂ is at most degree-1 in the components of input vector, and J₄ is at most degree-2. The above paper near the top of page 6 in the right-hand column makes the claim that the following two conditions are equivalent 

∃ c, ∀ k : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3), ∀ K₀ : ℝ, ‖k‖ ≤ 1 → 0 < K₀ → c ≤ J₂ k * K₀ + J₄ k * K₀²

and

∀ k : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3), ‖k‖ ≤ 1 → ((0 < J₄ k) ∨ (J₄ k = 0 ∧ 0 ≤ J₂ k))

This is demonstrably false, with J₂ k = k 1 and J₄ k = (1 - k 0)² forming an explicit counter example (satisfies the second but not the first). Theorem 1 of that paper is in part equivalent to a reworking of this condition.

Very impressive work! I believe it has the potential to become the paradigm for future hep-ph research. Before I ask a question about the methods in this paper, I noticed it says: "the project PhysLib [2] (recently renamed from PhysLean [3] to merge with the Lean-QuantumInfo library [4, 5])". Has the merge already been completed, or has it just been initiated?

Right now all the changes (besides the name) are behind the scenes. Physlib is currently just what was PhysLean and I don't believe anything has been merged yet. Lean-QuantumInfo is finishing up some existing work in progress and then will start to be merged into Physlib.

@Daniel Morrison
Thank you for the clarification. We are planning to use Lean-QuantumInfo in our agent, but there is a version conflict. It would be great if Physlib could include it—we could then use it directly.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/2520546-computer-finds-flaw-in-major-physics-paper-for-first-time/ :tada:
https://archive.is/6N8tC
Oh did the original authors respond? Curious how that interaction went and if they commented on the use of lean

Yep they responded: confirmed that there it is indeed an error in their paper in the "marginal stability" case, said they admire the power of the tools for computer checks, and would be writing an erratum. I've also since had a great interaction with Igor Ivanov who works in this area, to confirm similar things.
(Also just to make it clear - apart from a 10min conversation with the journalist I had no other input into this New Scientist article)

Hi Joseph, I saw you another paper on SU(5) Model Building which is also cool. Your framework elevates "absence results" to theorem-backed guarantees at the charge-spectrum layer; do you envision the same API scaling to formalize no-go theorems at higher layers? But no-go theorems are sometimes "dangerous", have you consider how to deal with them?

Hey @Jinzheng Li, if you mean "can you exclude theorems by things other than charge spectra using the same sort of methods" - then I'm sure the answer is yes, we have examples of this where we add things like fluxes to the matter curves. There is likely a limit to this, and some situations where it would not work. I'm not sure in what context you mean "dangerous" here?

@Joseph Tooby-Smith

Thanks — yes, that is what I meant. By “dangerous,” I mean that no-go theorems can be overgeneralized: Lean-style formalization helps by making the assumptions much more explicit, so the exclusion statement becomes less easy to oversell. But there is still a hidden-assumption problem at the modeling level — one can formalize the theorem correctly while still missing that the physical setup itself was too narrow. Goldstone’s theorem is the classic example: the no-go looked much stronger than it really was because the underlying assumptions did not cover the gauge-theory case.

Yeah, I agree here, if the assumptions are incorrect or too narrow at the physical level, Lean isn't going to help you much, apart from making this more apparent, and therefore easier to check. With these things, one can always try and move the assumptions back to something more fundamental, and use that as a check of the validity of the physical starting point.
